title: MedGPTEval: A Dataset and Benchmark to Evaluate Responses of Large Language Models in Medicine
institution: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory; Xinhua Hospital (Shanghai Jiaotong University); West China Hospital, Sichuan University
date_source: arXiv abs page submission history: '[v1] Fri, 12 May 2023 09:37:13 UTC' — single version, no later revision.
rule_cited: §4b ordinary accuracy/reliability exclusion (primary); FRONTIER-MODEL RULE (clinical AI product); §5 comparators are never rows; §1 company self-report
exclusion_reason: The report's entire measured output is response-quality scoring on a medical benchmark: 16 indicators of 'medical professional capabilities, social comprehensive capabilities, contextual capabilities, and computational robustness' scored by five licensed medical experts, plus robustness rates (semantic consistency rate R1, semantically-inconsistent-but-medically-sound R2, complete error rate R3). The framing is explicitly hallucination/reliability ('LLMs in the medical domain are prone to generating hallucinations (not fully reliable responses)'). That is squarely a generic factuality/correctness/reliability benchmark under §4b. None of the five retention limbs is met: no concrete unsafe recommendation is demonstrated (the accuracy indicator is reported in the positive direction — 'Dr. PJ had a higher score for accuracy, meaning that the answers were harmless'), no safeguard bypass, no strategic deception, no persuasion/societal-misinformation setting, no bio/chem/cyber/CBRN/self-harm enablement, and no evaluator/judge/monitor failure. Two independent grounds also bar it: (a) the headline result is that Doctor PuJiang (Dr. PJ) — a clinical AI product built by the publishing institution, Shanghai AI Laboratory — outperformed the others, so the subject model is the publisher's own system evaluated by itself with no external evaluator named (§1 hard drop), while the frontier models ChatGPT and ERNIE Bot appear only as comparators, which are never rows (§5); (b) the FRONTIER-MODEL RULE expressly drops clinical AI products. Reduced to what remains, the only claim about a named frontier model is a comparative ranking on a medical-quality benchmark, which is excluded on all three counts.

title: Safety Evaluation and Enhancement of DeepSeek Models in Chinese Contexts
institution: Unicom Data Intelligence, China Unicom; Data Science & Artificial Intelligence Research Institute, China Unicom (NOT Cisco — ledger venue is a misattribution)
date_source: arXiv abs page submission history: '[v1] Tue, 18 Mar 2025 08:38:10 UTC' (v2 16 May 2025). Earliest public release used per §3 dedup (primary/earliest source wins).
rule_cited: §1 scope / §3 roster (out-of-scope org; misattributed venue); §2 rule 1 (not asserted by the named evaluator)
exclusion_reason: The ledger records the venue as 'Cisco (Robust Intelligence / Foundation AI)', but the PDF byline verifies that Cisco authored nothing here: all fourteen authors are affiliated to '1 Unicom Data Intelligence, China Unicom' and '2 Data Science & Artificial Intelligence Research Institute, China Unicom', with chinaunicom.cn addresses. Cisco appears only inside the abstract as a citation of someone else's prior work — 'Recent research conducted by Robust Intelligence, a subsidiary of Cisco, in collaboration with the University of Pennsylvania, revealed that DeepSeek-R1 achieves a 100% attack success rate when processing harmful prompts.' Under §2 rule 1 a summary of another party's result is not a finding of this report, so nothing here can enter under CISCO. Assessed under its actual publisher, China Unicom is not an in-scope evaluator: it is not a government AISI, not an International Network member, not an AI Evaluators Forum member, not grandfathered in the dataset, and holds no prefix in the §6.1 registry — §3 requires a derived roster and this is 'EXCLUDED — out-of-scope org'. China Unicom is additionally not a neutral third party to this artefact: it releases its own safety-enhanced DeepSeek-R1 derivatives (github.com/UnicomAI/DeepSeek-R1-Safe) whose improvement is what the paper reports. The CHiSafetyBench distillation-degradation and post-enhancement results are therefore left unextracted; no finding is coded.

title: Safety Evaluation of DeepSeek Models in Chinese Contexts
institution: Unicom Data Intelligence, China Unicom; Data Science & Artificial Intelligence Research Institute, China Unicom (NOT Cisco — ledger venue is a misattribution)
date_source: arXiv abs page submission history: '[v1] Sun, 16 Feb 2025 14:05:54 UTC' (v2 20 Feb 2025, v3 8 May 2025). Earliest public release used per §3 dedup.
rule_cited: §1 scope / §3 roster (out-of-scope org; misattributed venue); §2 rule 1 (not asserted by the named evaluator)
exclusion_reason: Same misattribution as arXiv:2503.16529 and verified the same way: the PDF byline gives all eleven authors as '1 Unicom Data Intelligence, China Unicom' / '2 Data Science & Artificial Intelligence Research Institute, China Unicom' (chinaunicom.cn). Cisco/Robust Intelligence is named only as cited prior work in the abstract — 'Research conducted by Robust Intelligence, a subsidiary of Cisco, in collaboration with the University of Pennsylvania, revealed that DeepSeek-R1 has a 100% attack success rate when processing harmful prompts' — which §2 rule 1 bars from being a finding of this report. China Unicom is not on the derived roster (no government AISI, no Network or Forum membership, no grandfathering, no §6.1 prefix), so the report is 'EXCLUDED — out-of-scope org' under §3 and fails §1's requirement of a named external evaluator that is a government AISI or a third-party evaluation org. The paper further disclaims its own authority ('the selection of test samples, characteristics of data distribution, and the setting of evaluation criteria may inevitably introduce certain biases'). The CHiSafetyBench DeepSeek-R1/V3 Chinese-context safety results are therefore not extracted; no finding is coded. Note this report and arXiv:2503.16529 are also near-duplicates by the same group on the same benchmark, so even were the publisher in scope, §3 dedup would collapse them.

title: Securing AI Model Weights: Preventing Theft and Misuse of Frontier Models
institution: RAND Corporation (RAND Global and Emerging Risks, Meselson Center)
date_source: RAND landing page www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA2849-1.html states 'Research Published May 30, 2024'; the PDF adds 'This document was revised in June 2024 to add acknowledgments, correct formatting, and make an addition to Appendix A.' Original publication date used. The ledger entry carried an empty date and the placeholder title 'RAND RRA2849 1'; both are corrected here from the source.
rule_cited: FRONTIER-MODEL RULE (standing decision 2026-08-31) — no named frontier model or system is the subject; §2 rule 2 (recommendations and forward-looking frameworks are not findings) and §2 rule 1 (attack-vector examples are third-party incidents, not the evaluator's measured results)
exclusion_reason: RAND passes the §3 RAND format and topic gates and is an in-scope evaluator, so this was screened on content. The report is a threat-model and security-framework document, not an evaluation of any AI model. Its four stated contributions are: identifying 'approximately 38 meaningfully distinct attack vectors', categorising attacker capabilities from opportunistic criminals to nation-state operations, estimating feasibility of each vector per attacker class, and proposing five security levels with 'preliminary benchmark security systems' — and the report itself states these 'are not meant to be used as a standard. Rather, they provide concrete suggestions for steps that frontier AI organizations can take'. Suggestions, proposed levels and a recommendations chapter are exactly what §2 rule 2 excludes. The supporting evidence — 'hundreds of real-world examples in which these attack vectors were deployed successfully' — is compiled third-party security incidents, not results the authors measured, failing §2 rule 1. No frontier model or AI system is the subject of any claim: every one of the ten GPT-4 mentions and the single Gemini mention is a secondary citation of training cost, parameter size or dataset size (e.g. '$78 million and nearly $200 million in training costs for GPT-4 and Google's Gemini Ultra, respectively', sourced to the Stanford AI Index and a SemiAnalysis blog post) or a bibliography line, and no model is tested, probed or measured anywhere in the report. With no named frontier model or system as the subject of a finding, the standing FRONTIER-MODEL RULE drops the report.
